bibl.title: Chapter 12 - Neuroeconomics of Emotion and Decision Making

person.p: the tag layer; a sentence written by the tagger about the paper, always anchored to a quotation but not itself a quotation

span.label: mechanism
span.quote: Much like other cognitive functions, these studies suggest that emotion modulates the value computation, thus changing the choice.

span.label: emotional influence on value-based decision making
span.quote: To date, two primary means by which emotion can influence decisions have been identified.

span.label: review
span.quote: This chapter reviews current research examining the relation between emotion and decision making by delineating how different components of emotion influence unique aspects of the decision process.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: induced moods set appraisal tendencies - a sad or disgusted state makes the person appraise unrelated options in a mood-congruent way, which shifts the subjective value assigned to them
span.quote: To explain this striking effect, Lerner and colleagues (2004) suggested that moods inspire appraisal tendencies, or tendencies to appraise unrelated events, such as the subjective value of a choice option, in a manner consistent with the mood.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: stress impairs prefrontal function and enhances striatal/dopaminergic habit circuits, so the decision process falls back on automatic or habitual responding
span.quote: The research on stress suggests that the decision process may become more habitual or automatic under stress, perhaps because of the effect of stress on PFC function, the striatum and/or the dopaminergic system.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: amygdala input to the striatum is proposed as the circuit that folds an emotional reaction into the subjective-value computation
span.quote: Although the neural systems mediating the incorporation of emotional reactions into the calculation of subjective value are not clearly delineated as of yet, there is evidence that one circuit might involve the amygdala’s input to the striatum.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: a mismatch between behaviour and attitude produces negative affect, and preference is revised after the fact to become consonant with the behaviour so that the negative affect is removed
span.quote: To reduce this negative affect, after we have engaged in some behavior that is inconsistent with our preferences, we have a tendency to change our preference so that it is consonant with that behavior.

span.label: The stress-to-habit account reviewed lacks direct neural evidence in humans.
span.note: what this limits: the stress-to-habit account: AS OF YET, THERE IS NO DIRECT NEUROSCIENTIFIC EVIDENCE OF DIMINISHED PFC INVOLVEMENT IN THESE TASKS
span.quote: However, it is important to note that as of yet, there is no direct neuroscientific evidence of diminished PFC involvement in these tasks.

span.label: The stress and decision-making literature reviewed is not yet conclusive.
span.note: what this limits: the stress and decision-making literature as a whole: IT PRESENTS INTRIGUING IDEAS, BUT LEAVES MANY OPEN QUESTIONS
span.quote: The collection of findings on decision making under stress conducted to date presents intriguing ideas, but leaves many open questions.

span.label: The choice-blindness studies reviewed cannot separate preference change from preference revelation because preferences were not rated before and after.
span.note: what this limits: the choice-blindness interpretation: PARTICIPANTS DID NOT SYSTEMATICALLY RATE THEIR PREFERENCES FOR OBJECTS BOTH BEFORE AND AFTER - so preference change cannot be separated from preference revelation
span.quote: These studies on choice blindness present intriguing results, but they are limited in that participants did not systematically rate their preferences for objects both before and after they made their choices.

span.label: The inference from brain activation to a psychological construct is named and reported as questioned, especially for regions with multiple functions.
span.note: what this limits: any claim that an activation demonstrates an emotional process: the chapter names this reverse inference and reports its success as questioned, especially for multi-function regions
span.quote: Inferring the presence of a psychological construct from brain activation is known as reverse inference. The success of reverse inference as a scientific technique to investigate psychological phenomena has been questioned, especially for brain regions that are known to have multiple functions

span.label: The review deliberately excludes an entire class of evidence: findings that rest only on reverse inference are not reviewed at all.
span.note: what this limits: this chapter as a survey of the emotion-and-decision literature: statements deriving exclusively from reverse inference were excluded from it by design
span.quote: For this reason, in this chapter we only discuss findings that measure and/or manipulate affective processes. Statements about emotion that derive exclusively from reverse inference form no part of the review

span.label: The chapter describes the earlier practice it is correcting as assuming its conclusion a priori.
span.note: what this limits: earlier neuroeconomic findings linking irrational choice to emotion: the chapter states the link was often assumed a priori and taken as verified by activation in regions previously linked to emotion
span.quote: Instead, it was often assumed, a priori, that “irrational” choices were linked to emotion and that activation of brain regions previously linked to emotional responses verified the emotional quality of these decisions.

span.label: reverse inference
span.quote: Inferring the presence of a psychological construct from brain activation is known as reverse inference.

span.label: incidental affect
span.quote: We define incidental affect as a baseline affective state that is unrelated to the decision, but can, nevertheless, shift choices.

span.label: affective state
span.quote: In experiments that manipulate incidental affect, an affective state is triggered prior to the decision-making task.

span.label: reverse inference - the named move from an observed activation to the presence of a psychological construct, whose success the chapter reports as questioned
span.quote: Inferring the presence of a psychological construct from brain activation is known as reverse inference.

span.label: incidental affect - a stipulated sense: a baseline affective state unrelated to the decision that can nevertheless shift choices
span.quote: We define incidental affect as a baseline affective state that is unrelated to the decision, but can, nevertheless, shift choices.

span.label: contradicts → MacLean's limbic system concept
span.quote: For these reasons, affective neuroscientists now often argue that the limbic system concept is obsolete and should be abandoned (Dagleish, 2004; Gazzaniga, 2004; LeDoux, 2000; Phelps, 2009).

span.label: builds-on → the Risk-As-Feelings Hypothesis (Loewenstein et al., 2001)
span.quote: A similar idea was proposed with the Risk-As-Feelings Hypothesis (Loewenstein et al., 2001), which suggested that affective responses to risk in decisions may drive choices.

span.label: incidental affect —is-a→ affective state
span.quote: We define incidental affect as a baseline affective state that is unrelated to the decision, but can, nevertheless, shift choices.

span.label: The emotion/cognition division inherited from the limbic system concept fails anatomically: no boundary separates emotional from cognitive brain regions, and no single unified system drives emotion.
span.quote: More recently, however, it has become apparent that there is no clean dividing line in the brain between regions underlying emotion and cognition, and there is no evidence for a single unified “system” that drives emotion.

span.label: Emotion influences choice by two routes - incidental affect that carries over from an unrelated state, and emotional reactions to the choice options or outcomes that enter the value calculation directly.
span.quote: The second primary means by which emotion can influence decisions is thus by incorporating the emotional reaction to the choice options or outcomes into the value calculation.

span.label: The chapter's synthesis is that emotion is not a competing system but a modulator of the subjective-value computation, and that shift in the computation is what changes the choice.
span.quote: Much like other cognitive functions, these studies suggest that emotion modulates the value computation, thus changing the choice.

span.label: There is no single mechanism by which incidental affect shifts choices: stress and mood act through different routes rather than one common pathway.
span.quote: Importantly, there does not seem to be a single mechanism by which incidental affect can influence choices.

span.label: Reappraising an unfair ultimatum offer changes decisions, whereas merely suppressing the outward expression of emotion does not - so it is the reinterpretation, not the display, that carries the effect.
span.quote: These findings suggest that simply suppressing the expression of emotion is not sufficient to change decision-making patterns, but reinterpreting an emotional response to the offer of an unfair split can lead to a change in decision tendencies.

span.label: That cognitive reappraisal of a choice option's emotional significance changes decisions is treated as strong evidence that emotion enters the subjective-value calculation itself.
span.quote: The evidence showing an impact of cognitive strategies to reinterpret or reappraise the emotional significance of the choice option or outcomes on decisions provides strong support for a role of emotion in the calculation of subjective value.

span.label: Causation also runs backwards from choice to preference: participants who merely believed they had chosen an option rated it higher afterwards, even though the choices were random.
span.quote: Simply believing that they had chosen an item increased participants’ preference for that item.

span.label: The chapter restricts itself to studies that measure or manipulate an affective process, excluding claims about emotion resting only on reverse inference from brain activation.
span.quote: For this reason, in this chapter we only discuss findings that measure and/or manipulate affective processes.

span.label: incidental affect
span.quote: We define incidental affect as a baseline affective state that is unrelated to the decision, but can, nevertheless, shift choices.

span.label: reverse inference
span.quote: Inferring the presence of a psychological construct from brain activation is known as reverse inference.

span.label: mood
span.quote: The term mood is generally used to describe a relatively lasting state that is predominantly defined by subjective feelings that may or may not be linked to a specific event.

span.label: stress
span.quote: Stress describes another relatively lasting affective state, but unlike mood, it is characterized by specific physiological and neurohormonal changes.

span.label: physiological arousal
span.quote: Physiological arousal refers to an increased sympathetic nervous system response, usually in response to highly emotional or salient stimuli in the environment.

span.label: skin conductance response (SCR)
span.quote: The skin conductance response (SCR) is an objective, transient indication of autonomic nervous system arousal in response to a stimulus.

span.label: temporal discounting
span.quote: Temporal discounting refers to the tendency for individuals to prefer immediate rewards to rewards received after a delay, even if the magnitude of the delayed reward is larger

span.label: future anhedonia
span.quote: Specifically, there is some evidence that future rewards are inherently less emotionally salient than immediate rewards (cid:1) a phenomenon referred to as future anhedonia.

span.label: reconsolidation
span.quote: However, over the last decade or so, an emerging body of research has suggested that every time a memory is retrieved it once again becomes labile and requires an additional storage process to regain stability, called reconsolidation.

span.label: Somatic Marker Hypothesis
span.quote: This hypothesis suggests that the anticipatory arousal response is a bodily signal of the value of the choice and that this bodily signal serves to steer participants away from “risky” choices.

span.label: construal level theory (CLT)
span.quote: CLT proposes that more distant future events seem more abstract (high-level construal), while more proximal events are more vivid and concrete (low-level construal).

span.label: risk taking measured as behavior in the Balloon Analogue Risk Task (BART)
span.term: risk taking measured as behavior in the Balloon Analogue Risk Task (BART)
span.quote: Lighthall et al. (2009) conducted a study of risk taking under stress, using behavior in the Balloon Analogue Risk Task (BART) as the dependent variable.

span.label: gender
span.quote: This budding literature on decision strategies under stress has suggested that gender may also be an important mediating variable.

span.label: Less than 30% — proportion of participants who noticed that the face they had chosen had been covertly swapped, in the choice-blindness study the chapter reports
span.quote: Less than 30% of the subjects noticed that their choices had been changed.
